publisher: European Commission, Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development
title: Commission allocates €540 million in support to farmers facing the fertiliser and energy crisis arising from the Middle East crisis
date_evidence: Article header: "News article - 17 July 2026 - Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development"; foot of article: "Publication date 17 July 2026"; meta-og:updated_time: 2026-07-17T14:00:00+0200
key_claim: On 17 July 2026 Member States endorsed the Commission's proposal to mobilise €540 million from the agricultural reserve as financial relief for farmers hit by higher fertiliser and energy costs from the Middle East crisis, with national envelopes (France €107.1 million, Poland €66.6 million, Germany €60.3 million), a 200% national top-up option and a requirement to distribute the aid by 28 February 2027; the measure is one of the immediate actions of the 19 May 2026 Fertilisers Action Plan.
frame_summary: The Commission frames the reserve as a liquidity instrument for an input-cost shock, to be spent quickly so farmers can buy fertiliser for the 2027 sowing season; drought is not mentioned.
verbatim_quote: mobilise €540 million in financial relief for farmers affected by the Middle East crisis
verbatim_list: Today, Member States endorsed the European Commission's proposal to mobilise €540 million in financial relief for farmers affected by the Middle East crisis.

Member States may complement this EU support up to 200% with national funds. To ensure the effectiveness of this emergency measure, farmers should receive the financial support as quickly as possible. Member States should therefore distribute the aid by 28 February 2027.
To support them, it is necessary to provide targeted exceptional support to the farmers most affected through the agricultural reserve.
This initiative is one of the immediate actions set out in the Fertilisers Action Plan adopted by the Commission on 19 May 2026.

title: Exceptionally dry and hot weather threatens summer crops (JRC MARS Bulletin, August 2026)
date_evidence: Article header: "News announcement - 24 August 2026 - Joint Research Centre"; foot: "Publication date 24 August 2026 (Last updated on: 25 August 2026)"; meta-og:updated_time: 2026-08-24T14:00:00+0200
key_claim: Persistent heat and exceptional water deficits have cut EU yield forecasts for all summer crops to as much as 14% below the five-year average, with crop failure likely locally in France, southern Germany, northern and central Italy, Austria, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and western Romania; grassland productivity and pasture availability have declined markedly, raising fodder-supply concerns, and limited irrigation water and restrictions on its use aggravated the stress.
frame_summary: The JRC frames the season as a summer-crop and fodder event driven by heat and water deficit, with irrigation restrictions as an aggravating factor, and notes that late rain cannot recover the losses.
verbatim_quote: Grassland productivity and pasture availability have also declined markedly, raising concerns about fodder supply.
verbatim_list: Although summer crop conditions remain more favourable in parts of northern and eastern Europe, EU yield forecasts for all summer crops have been sharply reduced, falling below the five-year average by up to 14 %
Limited availability of irrigation water and restrictions on its use further aggravated crop stress in several regions.
Impacts range from moderate yield reductions to severe losses, with crop failure likely in the worst-affected regions.

title: Extension de la dérogation à l’interdiction de valoriser les jachères à tous les agriculteurs (communiqué de presse)
date_evidence: Dateline under the headline: "Mis à jour le 07/08/2026"; body: "Cette dérogation est possible à partir du samedi 8 août."
key_claim: During the July heatwave the French agriculture ministry allowed livestock farmers to harvest CAP fallow land to cover the fodder shortfall; given the exceptional length of the drought, the minister then obtained from the European Commission the possibility of extending that derogation to all farmers from 8 August 2026, so non-livestock farmers can harvest their fallows or open them to a neighbour's herd, on a force-majeure request to the DDT, for the whole 2026 CAP campaign.
frame_summary: The state services present the release of fallow land as the practical answer to the fodder shortage, an administrative derogation from CAP rules granted with Brussels' consent rather than a payment.
verbatim_quote: Au regard de l’ampleur et la durée exceptionnellement longue de la sécheresse actuelle, le Ministre de l’agriculture a obtenu de la Commission Européenne la possibilité d’étendre cette dérogation à tous les agriculteurs.
verbatim_list: Ainsi, les agriculteurs non éleveurs qui le souhaitent pourront valoriser leurs jachères en les récoltant ou en autorisant leur pâturage par le troupeau d’un éleveur. Cette dérogation est possible à partir du samedi 8 août.

title: New drought support for farmers
date_evidence: Byline: "Posted by: The Team, Posted on: 15 August 2026 - Categories: Drought support, environmental land management schemes, Grants"
key_claim: On 15 August 2026, with every county in England in drought or prolonged-dry-weather status, the government removed restrictions so all Environmental Land Management agreement holders can cut and graze scheme land to ease shortages of grazing, fodder, forage and bedding without losing payments, added £50 million to the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (total £290 million), offered up to £15 million for on-farm reservoirs and told the Environment Agency to prioritise short-term abstraction-licence variations.
frame_summary: Defra presents drought support as flexibility inside existing environmental schemes plus resilience grants, not compensation, and ties the package to a long-term water-storage agenda.

verbatim_list: As of 15 August 2026, all counties in England meet this criteria, meaning that all ELM agreement holders can use the temporary adjustments.

Funding up to £15 million to build on-farm reservoirs, helping farmers store water and become more resilient to future droughts.

title: GB milk deliveries: Milk volumes see further contraction
key_claim: GB milk deliveries fell an estimated 4.5% year on year in August 2026 to 992m litres as heat-stressed cows lost yield; milk-year-to-date supplies are 2.5% below 2025; forage growth is below the five-year average with some regions recording none, many farms have already started using winter feed, and the GB dairy herd contracted 2.2% in the 12 months to 1 July 2026 to the lowest level on record.
frame_summary: The levy board reads the August contraction as heat plus a forage gap that will run into winter, on a herd that was already at a record low, with processors raising prices to secure supply.
verbatim_quote: totalled an estimated 992m litres, a reduction of 46m litres (-4.5%) compared to the previous year
verbatim_list: Daily deliveries in August averaged 32.0m litres and totalled an estimated 992m litres, a reduction of 46m litres (-4.5%) compared to the previous year.
Forage availability in winter will be impacted following extreme temperatures and many have already started using winter feed.
The latest BCMS figures show that the GB dairy herd contracted 2.2% in the 12 months ending 1 July 2026.
This brings the milk year to date (April-August) supplies for GB to 2.5% below 2025 levels.
The GB milking herd continues to decline with the lowest level on record.

title: Planning for the rising fiscal costs of climate disasters (Policy Brief 13/2026)
key_claim: Low insurance coverage is turning EU governments into disaster insurers of last resort: direct losses from weather and climate extremes reached €822 billion between 1980 and 2024, a quarter of it in the last four years, and the six-country case studies of 2021-2024 floods and droughts show fiscal costs driven by ad-hoc allocations from public budgets; the brief argues for prevention, adaptation finance and a narrower protection gap.
frame_summary: Bruegel argues that ad-hoc post-disaster payouts are the expensive and unpredictable option and that the coming EU climate-resilience framework should shift the state from insurer of last resort to funder of prevention.
verbatim_quote: Narrowing the climate insurance protection gap so public budgets act less as the insurer of last resort.
verbatim_list: Climate-related disasters are affecting the public budgets of a number of European Union countries, with government spending replacing low insurance coverage in a context of more frequent and intense extreme weather in the future.
Low insurance coverage is turning EU governments into disaster insurers of last resort, strengthening the case for prevention and adaptation finance

publisher: La Via Campesina (European Coordination Via Campesina, ECVC)
title: Europe | Meeting with Hansen and Heydon: ECVC calls for immediate support to ensure no farms are lost
key_claim: After meeting Commissioner Hansen and Irish minister Heydon on 1 September, ECVC says the CAP crisis reserve, allocated €450 million a year, was used this summer mainly for the €540 million fertiliser scheme and is depleted during the drought; it asks for the reserve to be replenished, notes the Commission has already authorised advance payments of 70% instead of 50% from 16 October, and records that no commitments were made.
frame_summary: The peasant-farmer movement argues that the reserve was spent on an input subsidy that favoured large farms and that drought relief must be direct, capped per farmer and funded, framing the flexibilities as an abdication.
verbatim_quote: was used this summer mainly for a €540 million scheme covering synthetic fertiliser costs, leaving the reserve depleted during the current drought
verbatim_list: The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) crisis reserve, allocated €450 million annually to address emergencies, was used this summer mainly for a €540 million scheme covering synthetic fertiliser costs, leaving the reserve depleted during the current drought.
ECVC welcomes the fact that the European Commission has already authorised Member States to pay a higher percentage of CAP aid than planned (70% instead of 50% as of 16 October).
Despite our requests, no commitments have been made to change current policies.
